title: Quantum-Limited Blind Source Separation of Classical Light
abstract: Using the framework of quantum multiparameter estimation, we study the problem of separating independent thermal optical sources mixed by an unknown passive linear transformation, which is known as blind source separation in signal processing. We propose a sensing-assisted method that iteratively estimates and suppresses optical correlations directly within the unit cells of a programmable interferometer. We show that collective quantum measurements exhibit a substantial advantage over conventional detection methods by constructing collective measurements that asymptotically achieve the Holevo Cramér--Rao bound in a unit cell of the interferometer for the respective sub-problem. By systematically arranging multiple such cells in a photonic mesh, our proposal implements an in situ Jacobi diagonalization of the input multimode correlation matrix. We contrast our method with a conventional approach where heterodyne detection is used to reconstruct the full covariance matrix and subsequently diagonalize it on a classical computer. A comparison with this heterodyne tomography approach shows that our sensing-based method is particularly advantageous in the weak-light regime.
summary: This work tackles Blind Source Separation for thermal light by proposing a novel, sensing-assisted method implemented in a programmable photonic interferometer. This quantum approach estimates and suppresses optical correlations locally, achieving measurement precision superior to classical heterodyne detection methods, particularly when photon numbers are low.
main_problem: The paper addresses Blind Source Separation (BSS) for independent thermal optical sources mixed by an unknown passive linear transformation.
main_result: A proposed sensing-assisted quantum method achieves asymptotically optimal estimation bounds, showing a significant advantage over conventional heterodyne tomography, especially in the weak-light regime.
method: The authors propose an iterative, sensing-based approach implemented within a programmable interferometer mesh to perform an in situ Jacobi diagonalization of the input multimode correlation matrix.
model_or_system: The system involves thermal light sources whose output state is mixed by an unknown passive linear transformation $U$. The physical platform modeled is a photonic circuit utilizing tunable Mach-Zehnder interferometers as unit cells.
key_observables: Covariance matrices, correlation matrices, and quantum measurement outcomes like photon number differences ($\{P^{NDAB}_t\}$).
important_parameters: Thermal energies ($N_1, \ldots, N_K$), the weak-light regime (low photon numbers), and parameters defining the mixing transformation $(	heta, \phi)$.
main_assumptions: The theoretical framework relies on quantum multiparameter estimation theory, specifically comparing performance against the Holevo Cramér–Rao bound.
paper_structure: The paper develops the problem formulation using quantum multiparameter estimation bounds, proposes the sensing-assisted method via interferometer unit cells for iterative diagonalization, and contrasts this with classical heterodyne tomography approaches.
why_interesting: It demonstrates how fundamental concepts of quantum measurement theory (like achieving the Holevo bound) can be directly mapped onto physical hardware (photonic interferometers) to solve complex signal processing tasks like BSS.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Unit-cell sample-complexity comparison. The ratio kX/kspovm of copies required by method X and by the spin POVM is shown against B. Other constants such as the gap ∆, precision ε and confidence α cancels in the ratio, so the curves are universal. Similar regions of advantage were already observed in [63].

Figure 2: The ratio Nsens/Ng−het of the total number of copies required by the unit-cell-based Jacobi algorithm and by global heterodyne tomography on all K modes is shown as a function of the brightness B, for K = 16. The dashed line marks the break-even point Nsens = Ng−het, and curves below it indicate a region of potential quantum advantage. Ntdmapc and Nspovm reaches this region at low brightness.

Figure 3: Comparison of the heterodyne and quantum-optimal Fisher information for the beam-splitter angle θ, given by the ratio F het θθ /F Q θθ in Eq. (198). The left panel shows that the ratio is less than unity for all finite thermal occupations M, N. The right panel includes slices at some fixed N.

Figure 3 illustrates F het θθ /F Q θθ part of Eq. (198) over the full range of thermal occupations. The ratio is strictly below unity everywhere on the (M, N) plane, confirming that heterodyne detection is never optimal for estimating the beam-splitter angle at any finite occupation. Heterodyne detection approaches the quantum limit (ratio →1) only when both modes are bright, while the quantum advantage (ratio →0) is largest when either occupation is small.
